title: Bram and the Room
premise: Pest controller Sable Amberdale answers a call to her late grandmother's house, where the infestation is not insects but a room that shouldn't exist — a parlor that appears only in photographs, always with one extra chair. The room belongs to a thing that was wronged by the Amberdale family generations ago and now collects likenesses, counting the living toward a final tally it will complete at first frost. As Sable documents the phenomenon, she realizes the extra chair is meant for her, and that her grandmother made a bargain to defer the count. To end it, Sable must name the wrong publicly — a justice the law never delivered — and seat the family's confession in the chair before the frost finishes writing its final pattern, freeing the house at the cost of every photograph of her grandmother.
about_author: Noor Winterbourne is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed estate photographs and now writes horror about what those pictures keep. They live in a drafty farmhouse where they insist, cheerfully, that every room is accounted for.

chapters.title: The Call Comes From Inside the Listing
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, Sable's POV. Sable takes an odd job: a vacant estate house with 'activity' no exterminator will touch. She arrives with her documentation ritual — photos, notes, timestamps — and finds droppings that are actually small paper scraps of old family records. The emotional beat is professional calm beginning to crack into unease.

chapters.title: One Chair Too Many
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Reviewing her photos that night, she counts a parlor chair that wasn't there when she shot the room. Cross-checking her grandmother's old albums, she finds the same extra chair in decades of pictures, always slightly closer to the camera. The beat: dread arriving through evidence, her own language of proof turned against her.

chapters.title: What the Family Owed
chapters.summary: Alternating Sable's POV with excerpts from her grandmother's journal. Sable learns the house belonged to the Amberdales, and in 1931 a hired woman, Edith Marlow, was accused of theft, driven out in winter, and never heard from again — though the ledger Sable finds suggests the theft was the family's own. The beat: the horror acquires a history and a grievance.

chapters.title: The Room Opens for Visitors
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Returning at dusk, Sable finds the parlor door standing where no door was, warm air spilling out, the extra chair centered under the frost-ferned window. She documents it from the threshold; the room documents her back — a fresh photograph of herself appears on the mantel, seated. The beat: the watcher becomes the specimen.

chapters.title: Counting the Living
chapters.summary: Multiple short POVs: Sable's sister Priya, her nephew Dev, and an elderly cousin, each finding the chair in their own family photos, each feeling oddly summoned. Sable realizes the count includes the whole bloodline, and the tally is nearly complete. The beat: private haunting becomes family siege, and guilt becomes inheritance.

chapters.title: The Bargain Grandma Made
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, deep in the journal. Her grandmother found Edith's remains in the well in 1974 and buried the discovery to protect the family name, striking a bargain: one Amberdale life deferred per generation of silence. Sable's grandmother's death last spring ended the final deferral. The beat: grief curdling into anger at the dead for their cowardice.

chapters.title: Frost on the Inside of the Glass
chapters.summary: Sable and Priya's POV in alternation. The family gathers at the house on the coldest night of the season; frost spreads inward, spelling tally marks across every window. The room is now fully present, and Edith's presence — patient, wronged, terribly polite — asks only to be counted. The beat: the family confronts the cost of the name they carry.

chapters.title: The Chair Is Not a Punishment
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. In the parlor, Sable understands the chair was never a trap but a seat at the table Edith was denied — a place set for acknowledgment, not consumption. The thing takes likenesses only because no one would give it a name. The beat: terror reframed as an unanswered plea, and Sable chooses to answer it.

chapters.title: Read Into the Record
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, climax. Before the frost completes its final pattern, Sable reads the 1931 ledger aloud — the family's theft, the false accusation, the burial and its cover-up — and formally enters Edith Marlow into the family record as wronged, then seats her likeness in the chair herself. The room takes the confession instead of a life. The beat: catharsis through testimony, justice outside any court.

chapters.title: Everything Documented, Everything Released
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, weeks later. The parlor is gone; every photograph of Grandma now shows an empty, ordinary room, and the albums feel lighter, as if something was finally allowed to leave. Sable files her full documentation with the county historical society under Edith Marlow's name. The beat: quiet belonging — Sable keeps the house, keeps the record, and is at home in it.
